Learning Objectives
Determine the indications and contraindications for surgical management of lower extremity
metastatic disease.
Review the general principles and goals of surgical management of lower extremity metastatic
disease.
Describe common complications associated with the surgical management of skeletal
metastases about the femur and tibia.

Within the appendicular skeleton, bone metastases are most commonly localized to the femur
(specifically the proximal or subtrochanteric regions of the femur), followed by the humerus
and the tibia.1,2
Skeletal metastases are most often secondary to primary breast, prostate, renal, and lung
carcinoma and myeloma.1,2
Patients with skeletal metastases involving the lower extremity commonly report pain
(especially with weight bearing), limited mobility, or pathologic fracture.
Noninvasive or minimally invasive treatment options for bony metastases include radiation
therapy, cryotherapy/sclerotherapy, and systemic therapy (eg, chemotherapy and
antiresorptive agents).
The primary goals of the surgical management of metastatic disease in the lower extremity are
to relieve pain, restore mechanical stability, and improve function (allowing for immediate–
weight bearing and early motion).
Pathologic fractures do not have the same healing potential as non-pathologic bone
fractures;3 therefore, conventional osteosynthesis techniques may not be adequate.
Indications and Contraindications
The Snell and Beals criteria for impending pathologic fracture include lytic lesions larger than
2.5 cm and cortical involvement greater than 50% (circumference).
The Mirels scoring system predicts the risk of pathologic fracture based on the size of the
lesion, its anatomic location, and its radiographic appearance, as well as the presence/severity
of pain.
CT-based rigidity analysis (CTRA) recently was shown to be a better predictor of fracture than
the Mirels scoring system.
In patients with an impending or actual pathologic fracture, a multidisciplinary discussion
involving medical and radiation oncologists should be pursued; the discussion should focus on
the risks/advantages of surgical treatment versus less-invasive or nonsurgical treatment
options and on minimizing disruptions in systemic therapy.

Despite several attempts to define the risk of pathologic fractures associated with
skeletal metastases via a combination of imaging studies and/or clinical symptoms,
predictive ability remains poor, most likely because of the multifactorial effects of
heterogeneous cancers and the continued evolution of systemic therapies. One of the
first systems for predicting fracture risk was developed by Snell and Beals. In a cohort of
patients with metastatic breast cancer, the authors observed that the rate of femur
fracture was increased in patients with lytic lesions larger or equal to 2.5 cm that
involved the cortex.4,5 Subsequent studies defined fracture risk based on involvement of
the lesion within the affected bone rather than on absolute values. Fidler6,7 found that
the rate of pathologic fracture increased with involvement of more than 50% of the
circumference of the affected bone.
The Mirels scoring system, which remains the preferred method of predicting pathologic
fracture is based on lesion size on plain radiographs, the location of the lesion, the
radiographic appearance of the lesion, and the presence/severity of pain8 (Table 1).
However, the Mirels scoring system is controversial because of it is associated with
limited interobserver reliability and poor positive predictive value, with a tendency to
overestimate fracture risk.9

CTRA, a newer method for monitoring metastatic disease, defines an impending
pathologic fracture based on more than 35% reduction in axial, bending, or torsional
rigidity. In a study by Damron et al,10 CTRA outperformed the Mirels scoring system,
showing good accuracy in predicting the risk of fracture compared with fair or poor
accuracy with the Mirels system for all cutoff scores analyzed. CTRA may be useful in
surgical counseling for patients with lytic metastatic lesions in the lower extremity,
particularly the femur.
A comprehensive multidisciplinary discussion (involving medical and radiation
oncologists) should occur with every patient with skeletal metastases and a risk for
impending fracture if surgical treatment and/or less invasive treatment options and
systemic therapy are being considered. Surgical treatment may not be appropriate in
select groups of patients, including those with extensive medical comorbidities that
elevate the risk of perioperative mortality and those with a life expectancy of less than 4
to 6 weeks. Another relative contraindication is extensive metastatic disease elsewhere
in the body that may limit postoperative recovery (eg, extensive axial skeletal metastases
with spinal cord compression, large visceral burden, and progressive intracranial
metastases; (Figure 1).

(Reproduced from Swanson KC, Pritchard DJ, Sim FH: Surgical treatment of metastatic
disease of the femur. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2000;8[1]:56-65.)
Regardless, pathologic fractures of the lower extremity, particularly about the femur or
tibia, generally are managed surgically. Surgical treatment options range from
intralesional excision and stabilization with the use of plates, rods, and/or cement to en
bloc excision and reconstruction with the use of endoprosthetic implants. Treatment
selection depends on multiple factors, including histology, fracture location/pattern,
extent of metastatic disease (systemically and within the affected bone), medical
comorbidities, preoperative activity level, previous disease management, and anticipated
survival. A lesser trochanter fracture is considered a strong indication for surgical
management because of the high risk for fracture with disease progression in this high-
stress region of the proximal femur (Resources 1 and 2).
Techniques/Procedures
If metastatic disease in the lower extremity is managed surgically, the preoperative plan
should ensure the following:
A known diagnosis of metastatic bone disease or a biopsy confirming the diagnosis
Immediate mobilization and weight bearing
Decreased pain from bony metastasis
A reconstruction construct that will last for the patient’s lifetime given the histology of the
disease (Resource 3)
Preoperative Planning
If surgical management of skeletal metastasis is appropriate, the primary goals are to provide
pain relief and allow for early, full–weight bearing and range of motion.
For most skeletal metastases, surgical management is categorized as plate osteosynthesis
(with or without cement augmentation), intramedullary fixation, or endoprosthetic
reconstruction.
Several validated prognostic tools can help estimate patient survival, which is important in
balancing the durability of the construct with the invasiveness of the surgical procedure.


Preoperative Planning
A number of patient- and disease-specific factors should be considered during
preoperative planning for patients with metastatic disease involving the lower extremity.
If the origin of a skeletal metastasis is unknown, then a complete workup should be
performed preoperatively. If the primary disease is known, updated staging studies
should be obtained to characterize the full extent of metastatic disease because this will
affect surgical decision making. In addition, plain radiographs of the entire bone
involving the lesion of concern and any symptomatic areas. If additional sites of disease
are present within the same bone, these areas also should be addressed and stabilized
via the surgical construct. The fixation strategy should be based on the expected survival
of the patient, with the goals of allowing for early recovery with full, immediate–weight
bearing (when possible) and a durable construct for the patient’s lifetime.
Several validated prognostic tools—the Tokuhashi method,11 PATHFx model,12 and
others13,14—can help estimate patient survival (Resource 4). Their use in surgical
decision making is supported by the Treatment of Metastatic Carcinoma and Myeloma of
the Femur Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline published by the Musculoskeletal
Tumor Society (MSTS) in 2020 (Resource 5).
The use of adjunctive polymethyl methacrylate may improve axial and rotational stability
and screw pullout strength and reduce postoperative pain.15-17 In addition, preoperative
embolization may be considered in patients with hypervascular tumors, such as renal
cell carcinoma or thyroid carcinoma (Figure 2; Resource 6).

Surgical Approaches
Femoral Head and Neck
Most femoral head and neck metastases are managed via cemented hip hemiarthroplasty.
Long-stemmed cemented hip hemiarthroplasty has been associated with increased
perioperative and postoperative complications; however, the use of long-stemmed implants
may be indicated in patients with distal metastases observed on preoperative imaging studies.

Femoral Head and Neck

For lesions about the femoral head and neck, internal fixation generally cannot provide a
stable construct for immediate, full–weight bearing and is associated with a high risk for
implant failure or fracture. These lesions are best managed via hip hemiarthroplasty or
total hip arthroplasty. Hip hemiarthroplasty is most often recommended because of the
decreased risk for dislocation, the decreased surgical time, and the limited life
expectancy in this patient population (Figure 3). Occasionally, total hip arthroplasty is
indicated in patients with preexisting hip arthrosis or acetabular metastatic bone disease
(Figure 4). The risk for future conversion of hemiarthroplasty to total hip arthroplasty is
low.18,19

use of a long-stemmed, cemented, calcar-replacing hip hemiarthroplasty implant (B).
(Courtesy of Alexandra K. Callan, MD, Dallas, TX.)

Microscopic metastatic disease typically is managed via adjuvant radiation therapy.
Although noncemented femoral components may have a role in the management of
skeletal metastases,20 cemented hemiarthroplasty typically is performed because
pathologic bone and future postoperative radiation therapy may interfere with
osseointegration of press-fit implants. However, several studies have reported an
association between the use of cemented implants, particularly those with long stems,
and increased perioperative complications (including pulmonary embolism, cardiac
arrest, prolonged intubation, mental status compromise, and death).21-23 Other studies
have challenged this finding.24-26 Therefore, the major risks associated with the use of a
long stem should be balanced against the theoretic advantage of protecting the entire
femur. The MSTS 2020 evidence-based clinical practice guideline on the Treatment of
Metastatic Carcinoma and Myeloma of the Femur recommends the use of a standard-
length cemented femoral implant in most patients, with a long-stemmed implant

reserved for patients in whom additional distal lesions are identified within the femur on
preoperative imaging studies (Resource 5). If a long-stemmed implant is used, the
perioperative risks may be mitigated by venting the femur with the use of a distal drill
hole; copiously irrigating and suctioning the femoral canal before cementation; using
low-viscosity cement; and performing slow, controlled insertion of the implant.26,27 In
addition, clear and consistent intraoperative communication should be maintained with
the anesthesiology team during cementation (Resource 7).
Intertrochanteric/Subtrochanteric Femur
Surgical treatment options for intertrochanteric/subtrochanteric femoral metastases include
cephalomedullary nailing and endoprosthetic reconstruction.

Intertrochanteric/Subtrochanteric Femur
The proximal femur metaphyseal region, a common site of skeletal metastases, is
subject to high biomechanical stress. Therefore, prophylactic stabilization should be
strongly considered, even in patients who are asymptomatic. Surgical treatment options
include cephalomedullary nailing, arthroplasty, or segmental resection and
endoprosthetic reconstruction with proximal femur replacement (Figure 5). Each of
these treatment options allows for immediate–weight bearing postoperatively. The
primary advantages of cephalomedullary nailing include decreased surgical time and a
decreased risk for dislocation and abductor dysfunction compared with proximal femur
resection. If intramedullary nailing is selected, a long nail typically is recommended to
protect the entire length of the bone, regardless of the presence or absence of distal
metastatic disease. To augment fixation and potentially reduce pain, adjunctive
curettage and cementation may be performed in combination with cephalomedullary
nailing.15 Endoprosthetic reconstruction generally is considered a more durable surgical
treatment option.28,29

(A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the right hip of a patient with renal cell carcinoma

If proximal femur replacement is selected, purse-string capsule repair may reduce the
risk of dislocation30,31 (Figure 6). If total hip arthroplasty is performed, a constrained
liner may be considered. In patients with notably compromised proximal femur bone
stock or failed cephalomedullary nailing of a proximal femur fracture, proximal femur
endoprosthetic reconstruction typically is preferred28,29,32 (Resources 8, 9, 10; Videos 1
and 2).

Femoral Shaft
Femoral shaft metastases are commonly managed via intramedullary nailing or plate
osteosynthesis with or without cement augmentation.

Femoral Shaft
Impending or displaced femoral shaft fractures can be managed via
intramedullary nailing or a plate and screw construct, usually in combination
with lesion curettage and cementation (Figure 7). Antegrade nailing typically is
preferred, if possible; however, retrograde nailing also is acceptable for the
stabilization of mid-third or distal-third lesions. The use of a cephalomedullary
nail protects the femoral neck; however, a standard intramedullary nail may be
sufficient, with a study finding no evidence of subsequent femoral neck lesions
after intramedullary nail placement.33

metastatic renal cell carcinoma demonstrate hip hemiarthroplasty and open
reduction and internal fixation with the use of polymethyl methacrylate. AP
radiographs of the proximal (C) and distal (D) right femur of a patient with

metastatic urothelial carcinoma demonstrate management with the use of a
cephalomedullary nail followed by open reduction and internal fixation.
Cement-augmented fixation was not performed because of the permeative and
destructive lesion. (Courtesy of Alexandra K. Callan, MD, Dallas, TX.)
The risk for dissemination of metastatic disease during reaming and
instrumentation of the femur is currently being investigated; however, the
clinical importance of dissemination is not completely understood. A study
found that 25% of the reamings collected during femoral intramedullary nail
fixation for the management of impending or pathologic fractures contained
tumor cells, suggesting that the use of a reamer-irrigator-aspirator may limit the
theoretic spread of disease.34 A reamer-irrigator-aspirator also may facilitate
the collection of tissue for histologic confirmation and may decrease
intraosseous tumor burden and the risk of tumor emboli with canal
pressurization.
If a plate and screw construct is used, a laterally based locking plate is
recommended. To span the length of the femur, the longest plate option
available should be used, and all screw holes should be filled to increase the
stiffness of the construct and enhance stability in the event of local disease
progression. Plate fixation often is supplemented with polymethyl methacrylate.
This construct is ideal for stabilization of distal diaphyseal or metadiaphyseal
lesions. In addition, non-intramedullary nail device systems recently were
approved by the US FDA for use in the femur, tibia, and pelvis to stabilize and
supplement fixation constructs (Figure 8; Resource 11).

Distal Femur
Distal femur metastases are commonly managed via plate osteosynthesis with or
without cement augmentation or, more rarely, via endoprosthetic reconstruction with
distal femur replacement.

Distal Femur
The distal femur is the location of 10% of femoral metastatic disease. Surgical
management of distal femur metastatic lesions includes plate osteosynthesis
(typically with the use of a long, laterally based locking plate) with or without
cement augmentation, intramedullary nailing, or endoprosthetic reconstruction
(Figure 9). Similar to other femoral lesions, the construct should be selected
based on ; patient- and disease-specific factors, including the primary histology
of the disease, the patient’s estimated life expectancy and remaining bone
stock, and the specific region of the distal femur affected (including any
involvement of the articular surface). A useful algorithm for the management of
distal femur lesions, which considers some of these factors, was recently
developed in a systematic review of distal femur metastases35 (Figure 10).

Tibia/Fibula
Tibial metastases are observed less frequently than femoral metastases.
Surgical management of tibial metastases is based on the location of the disease and
the extent of articular surface involvement.

Tibia/Fibula
Metastases about the tibia and fibula are less common than metastases about
the femur. In a multicenter study of 592 patients with metastatic bone disease,
approximately 4.4% of long bone metastases were located in the tibia.36 Similar
to femoral metastases, surgical treatment options for tibial metastases
generally include intramedullary fixation, plate osteosynthesis with or without
cement augmentation, and total knee arthroplasty (Figure 11). Segmental
resection and endoprosthetic reconstruction with proximal tibia replacement

If a substantial amount of the articular surface is involved in a metastatic lesion,
modern modular revision total knee arthroplasty implants, including stems,
sleeves, and cones, may be used. Smaller symptomatic metaphyseal lesions in
the tibia should be managed via curettage and plate osteosynthesis and/or
cement augmentation (Figure 13), whereas diaphyseal lesions are best
managed via intramedullary nail fixation.

Ankle and Foot
Lower extremity acrometastases are rare; if they occur, they are commonly associated
with lung carcinoma and often are observed about the calcaneus.
Skeletal metastases about the foot rarely are managed surgically; however, if
indicated, management typically involves curettage and cementation with or without
internal fixation.

Ankle and Foot
Metastases are less common in the ankle and foot than in the long bones and
often occur secondary to lung carcinoma (22.7%), followed by kidney, breast,
colorectal, and genitourinary carcinomas.37 The foot bone most commonly
affected by metastatic disease is the calcaneus (31.1%), followed by the
phalanges, metatarsals, and talus.37 Surgical management rarely is indicated for
metastases in this region. If nonsurgical management fails, surgical
management typically involves curettage and cementation, possibly with
internal fixation (Resource 13).
Complications
Surgical management of metastatic bone disease is associated with an increased risk for
morbidity. In a retrospective review of more than 1,100 patients with femoral or humeral
metastases, 13% of the patients experienced one or more complications by 30 days
postoperatively. In addition, 33% of the patients required a blood transfusion, and 7.1% of the
patients died within 30 days postoperatively.38

Surgeons should expect increased rates of perioperative blood transfusion, deep vein
thrombosis (DVT)/pulmonary embolism, urinary tract infection, pneumonia, delayed wound
healing, and intraoperative death.
Metastatic bone tumors may progress postoperatively, leading to persistent pain and failed
fixation requiring revision surgery.

Complications
Overall, the complication rate in patients undergoing surgical treatment for metastatic
bone disease is higher than that in the general population. Several studies have reported
that the postoperative complication rate for metastatic bone disease was approximately
12% to 17%.1,38,39 The most common complications were DVT/pulmonary embolism,
infection or delayed wound healing, pneumonia, mechanical failure, dislocation, and
urinary tract infection. Postoperative blood transfusion frequently is necessary, with
reported rates as high as 33%. The risk for transfusion is higher in patients undergoing
arthroplasty/endoprosthesis and patients with renal cell carcinoma.38 Reported rates of
venous thromboembolic events have ranged from 2.5% to 12% in various studies.37,40,41
The physiologic effects of metastatic cancer and major orthopaedic surgery in the lower
extremity also increases the risk for venous thromboembolism in this patient
population. Appropriate chemoprophylaxis should be considered; however,
chemoprophylaxis is based on surgeon preference and, therefore, is variable. A recent
study reported no increased risk for wound complications with chemoprophylaxis for
DVT.41 In addition, the preoperative placement of an inferior vena cava filter is an
option, especially in patients with a history of DVT.
The risks and advantages of surgical treatment should be discussed with patients and
their family members. In a recent National Surgical Quality Improvement Program study
of more than 1,100 patients who underwent surgical treatment for metastatic bone
disease involving the femur or humerus, the mortality rate was 7.1% in the first 30 days
postoperatively.38 Although the goal of the management of metastatic disease in the
lower extremities is to improve quality of life and mobility, most orthopaedic oncologists
can recall a patient who died intraoperatively or before being discharged home (Video

Outcomes
Surgical management is not curative; it is intended to provide symptomatic relief to patients
experiencing debilitating bone pain or a pathologic fracture.
In this patient population, outcomes are improved with prophylactic fixation before a
displaced pathologic fracture occurs.
In patients with renal cell carcinoma, wide excision of a solitary metastasis is associated with
improved outcomes.
The goals of surgical management are decreased pain, improved mobility, and better quality of
life with continuation of systemic treatment.

As systemic treatment options and targeted therapy improve, life expectancy also increases.
The goals of surgical management should be modulated depending on histology and the
durability of the selected implant.

Outcomes
For patients with metastatic bone disease, surgical treatment is designed to promote
immediate–weight bearing and improve pain control. Many studies have reported
improved outcomes with prophylactic fixation of the long bone before pathologic
fracture occurs. Prophylactic stabilization of impending pathologic fractures also
improves pain and mobility while decreasing complication rates, hospital length of stay,
and the need for perioperative blood transfusion.41 Prophylactic stabilization also is
economically beneficial and cost-effective for the patient and hospital systems.41,42
Although surgical management is not curative for stage IV carcinoma, complete
metastasectomy improves overall survival, specifically in patients with renal cell
carcinoma. Several studies support wide excision of solitary bone metastasis in patients
with renal cell carcinoma to enhance overall survival.43-45 A study demonstrated
improved median cancer-specific survival in patients who underwent excision of all
metastatic sites (4.8 years compared with 1.3 years in patients who did not undergo
complete metastasectomy).45 In addition, wide surgical excision with endoprosthetic
reconstruction may improve functional outcomes and minimize the need for revision
surgery because of disease progression. Specifically, renal cell carcinoma is notoriously
radioresistant, with bony disease progression despite adjuvant radiation therapy and
systemic treatment options.
Although hardware failure is common in patients with renal cell carcinoma, implants
may fail because of local disease progression after fixation of any skeletal metastases.
Salvage options for hardware failure or symptomatic disease progression about the
proximal femur typically involve segmental resection and endoprosthetic reconstruction
(Figure 14).

The goals of surgical management of lower extremity metastatic bone disease in
patients with complete or impending pathologic fracture continue to be immediate–
weight bearing, rapid return to systemic treatment, and improved pain and function.
Augmenting fixation with the use of polymethyl methacrylate and/or locking plates and
the use of adjuvant radiation therapy is common. In patients with proximal femur
metastases, surgical treatment is associated with marked improvement in pain scores,
MSTS scores, and Karnofsky performance scores.46 Angelini et al47 reported improved
functional outcomes in 40 patients who underwent surgically treatment for proximal
femur metastases. All the patients experienced enhanced quality of life because of
reduced pain, and 77.5% of the patients were able to walk independently or with the use
of a cane at a mean of 2.5 months postoperatively. At final follow-up, the mean MSTS
score was 22.4.47
